questions.statement: Every morning my sister ___ to school at seven o'clock.
questions.context: Decide which tense describes a repeated daily habit.

options.feedback: Correct! A daily habit with an exact time uses the present simple, and the subject is third person singular, so the verb takes -s.
The present continuous suggests an action happening right now or around now, not a habit repeated every single morning.
The base form leaves out the -s that third person singular requires, so the sentence does not agree with the subject.
The present perfect links the walk to a period up to now, which is not what a fixed daily routine expresses.

questions.explanation:
The present simple describes habits, routines and permanent states. Because the subject is 'my sister', the verb must agree in the third person: walk becomes walks.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Last Saturday she ___ to the market and bought fresh cheese.
questions.context: Choose the past form of the verb 'go'.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Go' is an irregular verb, so its past simple is 'went', not 'goed'.
English does not add -ed to every verb; 'go' is irregular and its past form is 'went'.
'Gone' is the past participle, used after have, was or been, not the simple past on its own.
This mixes the auxiliary have with the bare form of go, which is not a valid past form.

questions.explanation:
Irregular verbs change their form in the past simple instead of taking -ed. Go, went, gone is the full pattern: went for the past simple and gone for the participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: While I ___ dinner, the phone rang.
questions.context: One action was in progress when another one interrupted it.

options.feedback: Correct! 'While' introduces a longer action already in progress, which is the past continuous.
The past simple would make the two actions a simple sequence with no overlap; the longer action needs the continuous form.
Cooking here happened in the past, so the auxiliary must be the past form 'was', not 'am'.
The present perfect links the action to the present, but the telephone rang in a finished past moment.

questions.explanation:
The past continuous sets the scene: the cooking was already under way when the phone rang. 'While' normally introduces the continuous action, and 'when' the short interrupting one.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I ___ in Tegucigalpa since 2019.
questions.context: The period of living began in the past and still continues.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Since' with a starting point in the past requires the present perfect.
The present simple would work only without since or for; with a starting date the present perfect is needed.
The past simple would place the action entirely in the past and suggest the living has stopped.
The past perfect looks back from another past point and cannot be used with since in this meaning.

questions.explanation:
Use the present perfect with since and for when a period started in the past and is still open now. I have lived here since 2019 keeps the door open on the present.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: By the time we reached the theatre, the film ___.
questions.context: Look back from a moment in the past to an even earlier event.

options.feedback: Correct! 'By the time' takes the past perfect because the film began before the moment of reaching.
The present perfect looks from the present, but the whole reference point is a past moment.
A bare past participle with no auxiliary is not a complete verb form in standard English.
'By the time' asks for the completed earlier action, and the continuous form here suggests it had not yet begun.

questions.explanation:
The past perfect is the past of the past. English orders the two past events and uses had plus participle for the one that happened first.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Look at those clouds. It ___ rain in a few minutes.
questions.context: Match the future form to the meaning of the sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! Visible evidence right now plus a prediction points to 'be going to'.
'Will' is used for predictions made at the moment of speaking, without prior visible evidence.
'Would' belongs to the past, to polite offers and to conditional structures, not to an immediate prediction.
The future continuous describes an action in progress at a future moment, not a prediction about rain.

questions.explanation:
Be going to predicts from present evidence, while will predicts at the moment of speaking. Dark clouds are evidence the student can already see, so be going to fits.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She ___ on the school project all morning and she still has not finished.
questions.context: The action started in the past and is still true now.

options.feedback: Correct! Present perfect continuous joins a past starting point to a still-true present result.
The present continuous would reset the action to now, losing the link with 'all morning'.
The present simple describes a habit, not an activity that began earlier and is still going on.
The past perfect continuous would look back from a past point, but the result is unfinished in the present.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect continuous is have plus been plus -ing. It emphasises that the activity started in the past and has not stopped, which is exactly what all morning describes.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: When I ___ tomorrow, the first thing I will do is call my mother.
questions.context: A time clause about the future must not use a future tense.

options.feedback: Correct! English uses the present simple in a time clause that refers to the future.
This is the error the rule exists to catch: a future form inside a when clause referring to the future.
The present continuous is possible for a fixed arrangement, but not as the general rule for a future when clause.
The past simple would make the clause refer to a moment in the past, which contradicts tomorrow.

questions.explanation:
In English a future time clause takes a present tense form: when I arrive, when you come, if it rains. The future idea already sits in the main clause.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: My uncle ___ a blue van and two bicycles.
questions.context: Some verbs describe states, not actions, and have no continuous form.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Have' is a stative verb here, so it keeps the present simple even in a sentence about a possession.
Stative verbs such as have, know and love do not normally take the continuous in this meaning.
The base form does not agree with the third person singular subject 'my uncle'.
The present perfect would point to an earlier acquisition whose relevance is still open, which the sentence does not express.

questions.explanation:
Stative verbs describe a state rather than an action. Used as possession, have cannot be made continuous, so the present simple is the only option here.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He ___ football every Saturday when he was ten years old.
questions.context: The activity happened regularly in the past but does not happen now.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Used to' marks a past habit that no longer holds.
The third person form of the negative is 'did not use to', never 'uses to'.
'Would' suggests a repeated action in a past context that can still be imagined as possible, not a habit that has ended.
'Be used to' is followed by a noun or a gerund and means being accustomed to something.

questions.explanation:
Used to plus base verb describes a state of affairs in the past that is no longer true. The question about when he was ten makes the past period explicit.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: By next December I ___ the whole English course.
questions.context: The action will be complete before a future deadline.

options.feedback: Correct! The future perfect looks forward from a future point to an action completed before it.
The future simple does not look back from the deadline; it places the action at or after it.
The present perfect looks back from now, not from next December.
'Would' belongs to conditionals and to past habits, not to a future deadline.

questions.explanation:
The future perfect is will plus have plus past participle. It answers questions like what will have happened by a certain future time, which is what by next December sets up.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He ___ a long letter when the lights went out.
questions.context: A sudden external event cuts a longer action short.

options.feedback: Correct! The past continuous gives the interrupted background action.
The past simple makes both actions equally short and separate, removing the sense of interruption.
The present perfect would claim the letter is finished and relevant now, but the story closes in the past.
A future form cannot appear in a sequence of events that the sentence presents as already completed.

questions.explanation:
The classic interrupted action pattern is past continuous plus when plus past simple. The long activity stays in the continuous while the short, unexpected event takes the simple past.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I ___ my passport, so I can book the ticket tonight.
questions.context: The marker 'already' signals a result in the present.

options.feedback: Correct! The result of finding the passport is still true in the present, so the present perfect fits.
The past simple would work with an explicit past time such as yesterday, but here no finished past time is given.
The past perfect looks back from a past point, and there is no past reference point in the sentence.
A future form contradicts the fact stated after 'so', which reports an already achieved result.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect is used when the past action matters because of its present result. Signals such as already, yet, just and never make the connection to now explicit.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: We ___ outside the school gate at six, so do not be late.
questions.context: A future arrangement has a fixed time and place already agreed.

options.feedback: Correct! The present continuous with a future time expression describes a fixed arrangement.
The present simple is used for routines and timetables, not for a personal arrangement made with friends.
'Will' would make the meeting a spontaneous decision taken at the moment of speaking.
The past perfect refers to a meeting completed before a past point, which has no place in this future arrangement.

questions.explanation:
A present continuous event that already has a day, a time and an agreement behind it is a future arrangement. It sounds much more definite than the bare future will.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ you visit your grandmother last weekend?
questions.context: Form the question in the past simple.

options.feedback: Correct! A past simple question uses did plus the base form of the main verb.
Do builds the present simple, so it cannot be used with a finished past time such as last weekend.
Were forms the passive, and this active sentence needs the ordinary do-support in the past.
Are is present tense support and would ask about a present state, not about a past visit.

questions.explanation:
When the past simple is a question, the auxiliary carries the tense and the main verb returns to its base form: did you visit, not did you visited.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Be careful! That glass is right at the edge. It ___ fall.
questions.context: The prediction is based on something already visible.

options.feedback: Correct! The evidence is in front of the speaker, so be going to carries the warning.
A will prediction is made at the moment of speaking, with no earlier evidence to justify it.
Shall is used mainly in offers and suggestions such as shall we dance, not for a prediction here.
A bare is does not build a future prediction; it would need a future form such as is going to or will.

questions.explanation:
Evidence already visible at the moment of speaking selects be going to. The warning only makes sense because the speaker can see that the glass is about to fall.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I ___ my grandparents this evening, so I cannot study tonight.
questions.context: The time expression places a present continuous action in the evening to come.

options.feedback: Correct! A present continuous with a future time expression describes a fixed personal arrangement.
The bare present simple would treat the visit as a general habit rather than one arranged for this evening.
The adverb later cannot replace the verb form, so the sentence would have no finite verb at all.
This is not wrong in meaning, but the continuous is the form that pairs with a definite future arrangement.

questions.explanation:
This evening is a future time expression, and the present continuous is the standard way to schedule it. The result clause explains the practical consequence for tonight.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: While the guide ___ about the history of the castle, a tourist asked a question.
questions.context: The action in progress is separated from the interrupting one.

options.feedback: Correct! The speaking in progress belongs to the past continuous, with the question as the interruption.
The past simple would reduce the speech to one finished act and destroy the sense of it continuing.
A present continuous cannot describe the past scene the while clause sets up.
The present perfect would push the speaking towards the present, but the whole story is placed in the past.

questions.explanation:
When two past actions overlap, the longer background one takes the past continuous and the shorter intrusion the past simple. While usually introduces the longer action.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He lives in La Paz now, but before the move he ___ in three different countries.
questions.context: Separate the state that holds now from the repeated past experience.

options.feedback: Correct! The past simple presents the repeated experience as a finished chapter of his life.
The present perfect would suggest he may still live in those countries, which the present sentence denies.
The past continuous would need a second past event to overlap with, and there is none here.
The past perfect would need a past point to look back from; 'now' is not that point.

questions.explanation:
The present simple states the current situation and but signals a contrast with a closed past period. The past simple is the right tense for that finished chapter.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: After she ___ the schedule, the class changed to the afternoon.
questions.context: Choose the form that follows the verb 'decided'.

options.feedback: Correct! A past main verb requires the base form of the verb that comes after it.
After a past tense verb the next verb returns to its base form; the present perfect cannot stand there.
The passive or continuous form breaks the rule that a sequence of past verbs takes base forms.
A future form after a past verb would mix two different time references in one clause.

questions.explanation: English does not inflect a second verb for tense. Once decided carries the past, everything after it appears in the base form: decided to change, decided that it would change.
questions.subject: ingles
